RETURN FROM ABROAD OF CANADIAN GRADUATE STUDENTS
speechtext:
1.	Has the attention of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration been directed to the recommendations contained in the report of Edward F. Sheffield and Mary Margot McGrail entitled "The Retrieval of Canadian Graduate Students from Abroad"?
2.	If so (a) has any action been taken to establish the Department of Manpower and Immigration as the central agency for the retrieval of Canadian graduate students from abroad, and (b) what, in detail is the nature of such action?
3.	Has any action been taken by the Department of Manpower and Immigration to compile and distribute information concerning Canadians studying abroad as recommended in the said report and, if so, what, in detail is the nature of such action and what distribution is given to such information?
4.	Has any action been taken to establish the Department of Manpower and Immigration as the agency through which guidance should be made available to Canadian gradute students abroad as recommended in the said report?
5.	If so, what action has been taken to make its role and services known to expatriate students through university placement officers, appointments boards, foreign student advisers and the like?
6.	If the answer to any of the foregoing questions is in the negative, what are the reasons for lack of decision or action?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. C. Munro (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: RETURN FROM ABROAD OF CANADIAN GRADUATE STUDENTS
speechtext:
1.	Yes. The Department of Manpower and Immigration has studied this report in detail.
2.	(a) Yes. (b) This year the Department of Manpower and Immigration has worked closely with the association of universities and colleges of Canada, the Civil Service Commission and representatives of Canadian industry, and professional associations, in establishing a program called "Operation Retrieval". Visits were made to 27 American universities and eight universities in the United Kingdom and western Europe, where substantial numbers of Canadians are studying. Each university was visited by a team made up of representatives from the association of universities and colleges of Canada, the Civil Service Commission, and the Manpower and Immigration Department.
The purpose of these visits was to provide Canadians studying at these institutions with information on career opportunities in Canada. During these visits personal information forms were given to all those who wanted to contact Canadian employers. These forms are being returned to the department for distribution to prospective Canadian employers.
[Mr. Laing.l
For the past three years the association of universities and colleges of Canada has sponsored a series of tours to American and British universities, initially to inform Canadian postgraduate students about academic vacancies in Canadian universities, and then gradually about a broader range of job opportunities. The department helped to finance the teams last year; this year it financed the visits, provided a representative for each team, and arranged a one day briefing conference for the team members.
The Department of Manpower and Immigration and the association of universities and colleges of Canada have agreed that in future the department will assume full responsibility for planning and administering similar programs for this purpose.
3.	Yes. The Department of Manpower and Immigration publishes detailed information on Canadians studying abroad in the form of two directories; namely, the directory of Canadian students studying in the United States, and the directory of Canadian students studying in the United Kingdom. The directories list each student's name, address, degrees earned, degrees expected, expected year of graduation, name of university attended, field of study, and, in the case of graduate students, thesis topic and supervisor.
The directories are available from the department without charge, and are sent at present to a mailing list of some 2,500 representatives of education, industry, professional and scientific organizations, and federal, provincial and municipal government departments and agencies.
4.	Yes. Please see the answer to part 5.
5.	Each visiting team held a general meeting to which all Canadian graduate students were invited, and followed it with a full day of individual interviews. The teams were equipped to provide professional guidance and occupational information.
In addition to the visiting teams, about 7,000 copies of the Canada careers directory were mailed to Canadians studying in the United States. This directory is a useful guidance tool which provides information on employment opportunities.
By means of the activities described in 2(b) and 3, an increasing number of Canadians studying abroad, university placement officers, and student advisers are becoming aware of the services offered by this department.
6.	Not applicable.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the serious housing crisis in Canada today, as evidenced by the disastrous drop in housing starts, high mortgage rates and the crippling rise in the prices and the rents of homes.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ALLEGED CRISIS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Would the hon. member for Danforth address the Chair on the question of urgency of debate.

subtopic: ALLEGED CRISIS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I shall be very happy to take the opportunity to do so. As Your Honour knows, this is a type of motion which is rarely brought in the house.

subtopic: ALLEGED CRISIS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ALLEGED CRISIS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Only when there is a matter which is felt to be of great and pressing urgency requiring debate is such motion brought. One of the requirements for debate is, as in this instance, that the subject matter of the matter to be debated be within the
Housing
ambit of government ministerial responsibility. Of this there is no doubt. The government is involved, perhaps inadequately, but it is involved in the matter of housing.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the hope that the Minister of Fisheries is in a better humour today than he was the other day I should like to ask him now whether he has received a request from the national Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Animals for the banning of the cruel and harmful killing of baby seals, and whether that society's representation has softened his resistance to action in this regard.

subtopic: REQUEST FROM HUMANE SOCIETY FOR ABOLITION OF SEAL HUNT
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker; Friday evening I received a telegram from Mr. A. L. MacLaurin, president of the Canadian Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. I was not surprised to receive this telegram, because the day before the seal hunt started he sent a circular letter to Canadian newspapers saying that he would ask for the complete abolishment of this operation.
The following was my reply to Mr. Mac-Laurin's telegram:
In reply to your telegram of March 17 I shall examine the written report of your observers St. Onge and Johansson in the light of information received from my officers and from the group of representatives of Canadian and international societies to whom we gave transportation. In spite of conflicting reports including some from irresponsible persons it is clear that conditions in the seal fishery in 1967 were improved by revised regulations and intensive enforcement and are comparable or perhaps better than in many activities involving the killing of animals. Mr. Chairman, as I recall the committee hearings, no firm opinion was expressed in connection with the clause now before us. It appears that during the last 15 years a flexible reserve of between 8 and 12 per cent has been in existence in accordance with the Bank Act. The evidence before the committee showed that although during all those years there was the possibility of change, it was in fact unnecessary to do so. The other reserves were fixed on the basis of persuasion and varied from time to time in accordance with the wishes of the governor of the Bank of Canada. The banks themselves agreed to vary their secondary reserves.
One of the recommendations of the committee covers a multitude of sins in connection with the Bank Act. It is only fair to say there are a good many things we cannot anticipate because we do not know what the future will bring. With the idea, therefore, that experience will teach us along the way, the committee suggested in its report-I should like to read this recommendation in order to bring some substance to the position I take-that a different approach be made. It said:
Your committee recognizes the value of regular or decennial revisions of the Bank Act, the Bank of Canada Act, and the Quebec Savings Banks Act but believes that these should not prevent this committee carrying out special studies on subjects related to these Acts, and amendments being made to them from time to time if such become necessary in the interval.
We could dispute long and loud in this committee on many fine points with regard to which we have no experience which would enable us to form an opinion whether we were indeed taking the best possible course. The recommendations of the committee, if carried out, would meet this problem. As soon as it was found that something in the Bank Act needed revision the necessary adjustments could be made. In the light of the evidence before the committee that opinion on this particular matter has not crystallized I would just as soon wait, let the Bank Act function, and then put the matter before the committee if hardship arises or corrections need to be made.

Indeed, I would say that if the governor of the Bank of Canada is the source of the advice upon which this amendment is based, and I suppose he is, he has gone quite a long way in recommending a reduction from 8 per cent to 6.6 per cent in cash reserves, and I would be altogether opposed to the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Edmonton West.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, further with regard to this amendment designed to reduce a bank reserve from 12 to 8 per cent of its deposit liabilities payable on demand in Canadian currency, it seems to me the hon. member could have submitted his amendment in another form, so as to require the Bank of Canada to give 100 per cent credit and banks to have a 100 per cent reserve when they make loans.
I wish to call the minister's attention to section 72, as well as to the amendment.
Suppose that I applied for a $1000 loan at a chartered bank and the manager complied with my request or accepted my guarantees for a $1000 loan, not one bank account is affected then. Other people's accounts are not reduced when mine is opened.
I deposit the $1000 in my savings account, and then chartered banks are allowed to use

that money as a 12 or 8 per cent reserve. This also enables them to multiply my loan by 12J, or 8, depending on the reserve rate.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Therefore, possibilities are practically unlimited, since chartered banks are in no way restricted from lending any amount. There is no limit because through the credit created it is still possible to create deposits, deposit liabilities. I appreciate the interaction of debit and credit, but the debit, or what I owe, is $1000, and the bank has the right to loan $12,000 even though my savings account amounts to $1000. That is how Canada, the whole country, is financially controlled.
Rather than requiring through an amendment an 8 per cent instead of 12 per cent reserve of the deposit liabilities-the banking system is given even more power-I believe the Bank of Canada should be ordered to create the credit necessary in the country. I do not see any danger of inflation, in spite of the fears often expressed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp). Why should there be more inflation if the Bank of Canada created credit instead of the chartered banks?
There is inflation now, when the chartered banks are told they may multiply their deposit liabilities by 12 or by 8 and charge interest on them. That interest is then definitely inflationary. It is the present system which creates inflation, not our suggestion that the Bank of Canada, which is our financial institution, should be used.
Mr. Chairman, I feel it is useless for us to accept this amendment which seeks to lower the reserves of the chartered banks from 12 to 8 per cent, especially when we, members of the Ralliement Creditiste, are fighting in this house against this financial control which is in the hands of a group of individuals.
We are discussing legislation which will be in force for the next ten years and we are asked to adopt the whole thing in a flash. It is much more serious than that, Mr. Chairman, and the amendment of the hon. member for Edmonton West cannot be accepted by us at this time.
What we are asking is that the Bank of Canada control the issue of money, credit and money supply in Canada instead of leaving this privilege in the hands of a group of private citizens called the chartered banks of Canada.
I think the minister could tell us at this point what is the limit of the banking system
March 20, 1967

at the present time? There is no limit, even though it may be set at 12, 10, 8, or 4 per cent, it does not matter if the chartered banks are allowed to use their deposit liabilities as reserves with the Bank of Canada to multiply it later 8, 10, 12 and even 15 times. There is no limit because any credit coming out of, or accepted by the bank may, through a simple gesture, or by pen being put to paper, create deposit liabilities from the very moment the loan is granted and thus create inflation.

subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this amendment of the reserves of chartered banks cannot be considered separately, without reference to the part reserves play in the operations of chartered banks.
The hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), after many other Social Credit speakers, raised the problems of reserves, 100 per cent at the chartered bank level, and by the same token stated that the central bank should assume full responsibility for the national debt instead of chartered banks.
Those two proposals go together. They have been put forward many times in this debate by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) and they would simply result in a situation where chartered banks would be obliged to have on deposit with the central bank or in cash one dollar for every dollar loaned.
Then, instead of what we have known for centuries, bank credit would simply replace the old bank-note method for transactions. We would have banks which from now on would merely make entries in their books, that is which would place at the disposal of the population an instrument of credit that would be exactly the same as the bank-note was for all transactions previously.
Replacing bank-notes by bank credit has allowed not only for an increase in currency to do business but also made it possible to do it more easily, and even from afar, and for huge amounts, etc. Everyone agrees that it has meant progress in the banking field throughout the world.
That is why the chartered and commercial banks must be allowed to maintain credit instead of keeping the old methods used in the past.
But to enable the chartered and commercial banks to continue doing business, they must be left free to some extent to grant credit as they see fit to those seeking it.
And, as a matter of fact, clause 72 now under consideration sets the reserves that our
Bank Act
chartered and commercial banks should keep. As stated earlier, the present method provides for a limit that ranges from 8 to 12 per cent; some variation was possible, depending upon the authority given to the central bank. According to the legislation introduced in this house. This reserve is now divided into two categories, one for demand deposits and one for term deposits.
The total effect of this variation, of this increase from eight to 12 and of this drop, in the other case, from eight to four, is that the average reserves will, in the present circumstances, amount to about 6.6 per cent. Therefore this means a drop in the average reserves of the chartered banks as a whole. This drop will, of course, allow the chartered banks, with their present reserves, collectively to create more bank credit or to facilitate credit. Of course, everything will depend upon the attitude of the central bank, following the enactment of this legislation, with respect to the reserves which will be left in the hands of the chartered banks. Either by its authority over the variation of the reserves, or by another and more usual operation which is called the open market policy and which involves the purchase and sale of government issues on the market, the central bank will still be able to siphon part of the reserves available to the chartered banks.
At any rate, to form an opinion on the reserves available to the chartered banks, one has to remember how financial reserves are meant to be used.
Their first and most obvious use, which strikes us immediately and which was emphasized by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), is that of liquidity. In other words, the chartered banks are required to keep part of their assets in the form of cash deposits at the central bank so that should customers ask that their deposits be converted into liquid money, the chartered bank will be able to fulfil its obligation toward its depositors. And just from the point of view of liquidity, it must be said that the reserve should exceed the normal needs of the customers with regard to the conversion of their deposits in bills.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
That purpose of liquidity also forces the banks to keep their reserves as low as possible, due allowance being made for its needs, to ensure as well reasonable profits.
Now, that is but one of the purposes of the bank reserve. The other purpose, on which

Should the reserves be too high, or too low, the efficiency of the central bank with regard to the chartered banks is threatened. The authorities of the central bank recommended to the committee a rate of 12 per cent in the case of deposits on demand as the one which best guaranteed its efficient control over chartered banks with regard to their assets on demand; and a reserve of 4 per cent in the case of term deposits as sufficient to ensure the central bank's efficient control over chartered banks.
Therefore, we see that the subdivision of the two rates is made because the behaviour of chartered banks is different and also because the effectiveness of the central bank control depends on whether it is based on term deposits or on demand deposits. Finally, it is because such reserves are also closely related to what is called the handling of the public debt.
In view of the fact that this is the most current and most effective method used by the central bank to exercise its own control, which is essential, in view of its functions with regard to chartered banks, the handling of the public debt, that is the purchase or the sale of government securities on the market, for the very purpose of creating reserves or of removing reserves within the portfolios of chartered banks, is absolutely essential within the present structures. So, it is essential that such determination of reserve rates be the same for all chartered banks. In view of the existing portfolios at the central bank level, it is essential that such determination be made here in the light of the objectives that the central bank may have in connection with

the interest rates which must exist within the economy itself as a whole, because all this is related. The central bank can in no way handle the public debt without first affecting the reserves of the chartered banks and causing a substantial fluctuation of interest rates on the market. Now, as those interest rates are very closely related to the yield of government bonds on the market, it is absolutely essential that the determination of the reserves of chartered banks should take into account the effects which the measures taken by the central bank to maintain such legal rates might mean. He is referring to the doctrines that he does not understand. If you can figure that out, you are better than I. I should like to read another quotation from the remarks of the minister as found on page 13371 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to reply to the young, amiable and handsome member who has just asked the question that the statement made by the premier of British Columbia is, so far as I know, without foundation. I would categorize it as both absurd and without foundation.
We have heard a lot about co-operative federalism. We have heard a lot about how the provinces should get along with the federal government and how the federal government should get along with the provinces. The minister's portfolio, of course, in essence

is a product of the getting together of the provinces and is not something which got the provinces together. I suggest to the minister that the use of sarcasm and ridicule is no way to find a solution to problems. I should like to read again from Hansard, page 13111:
-this is the sort of program that one might expect the Social Credit party to propose since they believe in a different form of financing, one that would be very inflationary and under which they would simply print money.
I should like to know what Social Credit material he has been reading. He says he cannot understand it, wonders how anybody can believe it, and then proceeds to say that it would be very inflationary in that we would simply print money. How does he know if he does not understand it. I should like to know who, in the Social Credit party, at any time advocated the printing of money. I have read items in the newspapers which have suggested that this is what we are advocating. I have been a Social Crediter since 1934 and I have never heard a Social Crediter advocate that we print money indiscriminately by means of a printing machine. This is something which has been suggested in the United States by none other than Mr. Anderson who at one time was secretary of the United States treasury. He suggested that this might be a good solution. The Social Credit party in this country has never recommended this.
I should like to deal with this question in retrospect. I go back to the time when we were in a depression, a time when people were being paid 10 cents a day to sit in a concentration camp, if you wish to call it that or relief camp because they did not have any money with which to do any purchasing. Retail stores across the country were amply supplied with goods for sale. I remember a storekeeper telling me that he had to keep a great deal more on the shelf because he could not afford to miss a sale.
What was the upshot at the beginning of the war? It was found absolutely necessary to increase the money supply greatly in order to fight the war. What was done in order to prevent inflation? I should like to go into this to some extent. In the first place, the government started selling victory bonds. They did not tell the people that the victory bonds were for the purpose of taking money out of circulation. They said it was to help fight the war. This was not the case at all. We know that. The victory bonds were sold for the sole purpose of taking money out of circulation which had already been pumped into the economy. It was already there and the expansion of credit was going on.
Bank Act
The next step was the introduction of war savings certificates. By this time the government was after the $5 bills. One could buy certificates for amounts as low as $5. In this way the government was able to take more money away from the people so they would not be able to spend it. Then the government introduced savings stamps in an effort to take more money out of circulation.
After having exhausted this procedure the next step was compulsory savings. No one could suggest for a minute that this was not proposed for the purpose of curtailing spending. Of course it was. I am not saying there was anything wrong about it. I am simply saying that these steps were taken by the government to prevent inflation inasmuch as the money supply had to be expanded in order to help the war effort. When compulsory saving failed to meet the demands rationing was introduced so that people would not be able to buy simply because they had money in their pockets. When rationing failed price controls were introduced.
At that time the man in charge of keeping prices down was one of the best men Canada has produced, Mr. Donald Gordon. He did a good job. During the war years the government did a good job in preventing inflation. They took the necessary steps. I am sure that if the minister would try to understand Social Credit he would understand some of the steps that were taken by the government in those days, because the concept of Social Credit is the converse of this. When the money supply is deficient there is a process by which money can be made available to the purchasers of the country.
I have heard it said that in Alberta and British Columbia the governments do not know anything about Social Credit and do not practice it. I can tell the committee that the concept of Social Credit is being practised directly in Alberta and British Columbia and now in the province of Saskatchewan. Right now in Saskatchewan a Liberal government is practising the concept of Social Credit. I make the statement this afternoon that if Saskatchewan, which is practising the concept of Social Credit, does not go ahead I will eat my shirt on the steps of the parliament buildings.

form of a secondary reserve to replace the agreements that the Bank of Canada has had with the chartered banks in the recent past. In this bill there is a well rounded and flexible system.

With the greatest respect, I still feel that the minister has missed the point of the proposal I put forward. At no time did I suggest that the variable rate should be above 8 per cent. We have that as a primary reserve. The secondary reserve is now being enshrined. All I say is that controls breed controls. That is my opinion of that.
What I should have liked to see is the additional facility open to the governor, in that he could move downwards from the primary rate-the primary rate of 8 per cent, 12 per cent, or whatever it is. This facility is not open to the governor at the present time; he is not authorized to go below 8 per cent. In the proposed act the rates are to be fixed at 12 per cent and 4 per cent and there are no deviations up or down. The government can move with respect to the secondary statutory reserve-perhaps one should call it the statutory secondary reserve-but that is a movement upward. Then, of course, he could come back to the former level. The flexibility is all in one direction, and that is the point I want to get across.
As an alternative tool I should like to see some downward flexibility in the primary reserves, rather than having that flexibility only in the secondary reserves. I do not think it is right to say that the governor had that power and he has not used it, and that therefore we are not impressed with it. The governor has never had the power to do this.

It must keep 8 per cent against deposits. A loan is made to an individual and it comes back as a deposit. Of course 8 per cent must be kept against that deposit.

The 8 per cent is reflected in the amount of credit which can be extended by the banks. Reducing it to 4 per cent will double the credit which theoretically the banks are able to provide. I think the best way of answering would be to say that these recommendations were made at a time when it was clear that monetary expansion had to be restrained. In other words, these changes are being made, not for the purpose of influencing the amount of money in circulation at the present time but to change the form of control over the money supply by relating it, not as in the past to 8 per cent of total deposits, but to 12 per cent of demand deposits and 4 per cent of notice deposits. The combined effect is somewhere between 6 and 7 per cent. It does indicate some reduction in the amount of reserve which needs to be kept against deposits.
If the hon. member will look at the clause under discussion he will see that there are transitional arrangements. In other words, we move in stages, month by month from the 8 per cent requirement down to the new minimum requirement, as provided for in clause 72(2) paragraphs (a) and (b). However, it would be the object of the Bank of Canada to exercise whatever might be the appropriate restraint or stimulation of the money supply as economic conditions dictate.
In other words, it is not the purpose of this amendment to enlarge the money supply or to restrict it. It is intended to change the way in which the Bank of Canada may influence the amount of the money supply. It is certainly not the purpose of this bill to enlarge the money supply. After all, the bill was brought in at a time when the governor of the Bank of Canada was concerned, as I was, about the money supply expanding too rapidly. He looked upon this bill as constituting a different form of control over the total volume of money in circulation, to be exercised in the light of economic conditions at the time the bank is making its decisions, operating in the open market or otherwise.

speechtext: In order to bring about an understanding between two individuals who are discussing a monetary problem it is necessary, before anything else, to define the terms used. What does the minister mean by "money supply"? Is it currency; is it money given by the Bank of Canada to the people? Is it hard currency or is it paper notes? If I go to the bank and borrow $1,000 I simply get a $1,000 credit on the books. I do not take any money out with me. I write cheques against my credit. What is the money supply? I think we must define that before it is possible to understand the minister's meaning.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: I have explained this on a number of occasions, both in committee and in the house. The money supply is the amount of currency, deposits in chartered banks and, to some extent, deposits in other institutions, against which cheques may be written. It is the total amount of money available for circulation whether through cheques or as currency.

speechtext:
Listening to the exchanges between the hon. member for Edmonton West and the Minister of Finance I was not sure whether the difference between them was one of degree or of kind. I gather that in any case it is a minor one.
My first reaction on looking at clause 72, and in particular at the provision for reducing the reserve requirements, was one of opposition. But I suppose a case can be made for reducing the reserve requirements, if for no other reason than to conduct an experiment under conditions of control. I think the decision to reduce the requirement by this small amount from 8 per cent to 6J per cent is not an imprudent one. I am a little puzzled by the position taken by the hon. member for Edmonton West. He seems to think that the clause does not allow for sufficient flexibility. It seems to me that the provision is such as to allow for the flexibility he believes to be desirable. The wording says clearly that the reserve requirement "Shall not be less than" and so on. Then it specifies what the minimum limit shall be. Beyond this there is, of course, room for discretionary judgment and variation on the part of the money management authorities.
Speaking more from feeling and instinct than from knowledge I cannot escape the impression that to the extent we reduce the reserve requirements we are giving to the banks greater discretionary power, and impinging upon the money management power of the central bank or of the public authority.

I see this kind of inverse relationship existing and I am not sure I like it one bit. However, as I say, the provision set out in the clause seems to be prudent enough. I look upon it as a kind of experiment within control, and on this basis I find it possible to support the proposal to reduce the requirements.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
Since I have not taken an opportunity earlier in this debate to speak about money management generally, I should like to take a few minutes in which to comment on some of the statements which have been made in this chamber in connection with this subject, particularly by those speaking for the Social Credit party and the Ralliement Credi-tistes. I am not one who has ever ridiculed their monetary theories or taken an opportunity to make fun of some of their basic propositions. Like the Minister of Finance I must say I really cannot pretend to understand all of Social Credit theory, but unlike him 1 have not, as I said, felt the urge to tilt at Social Credit theory with sword in hand. I believe it is possible to effect an expansion in the money supply without necessarily engaging a debt creating process. I do not want to get too involved with the immediate concept of debt creating but, after a considerable amount of reading and having interviewed some people who are in positions of authority respecting our economy and banking, I have come to the inescapable conclusion that, within limitation, it is possible, feasible, and practical to effect an increase in the money supply without necessarily bringing about an increase in debt.
What I mean is that it is simply no more inflationary to have the Bank of Canada take up government securities directly than it is for the chartered banking system to take them up. It is often said that one reason why we cannot entertain the prospect of the Bank of Canada taking up government securities directly is that this would have a direct inflationary effect, but the fact is that every time the chartered banks take up government securities there is an increase in the money supply.
Why should one kind of increase be inflationary and the other not? After persistent questioning on this point I have come to one hard bit of information: The main reason why there has been a reluctance or refusal on the part of central banks to take up government securities directly is that it would be psychologically disadvantageous. That is not a very satisfactory answer to hear, but it is the only one I have been able to get.
March 20, 1967

Before going to the point where I would be prepared to endorse the main body of Social Credit monetary thinking, I must enter one major caveat with respect to it. I do not apologize for taking the time of members of the committee in this way because this matter is one of the most central, crucial problems that face governments or any body of people elected to fill positions of public responsibility and trust. The one caveat I have to enter is that even if it were a matter of deliberate and conscientious government policy, and of central bank policy, to have central banks take up more and more government securities, this in itself would not ensure that the economy would progress without inflation and without interruption, because very often the problem is not one of inadequate supply of money or loanable funds. Very often it is a case of maldistribution of money and loanable funds within the economy, of a wrong distribution as between one industrial sector and another.
I can make reference to a specific case in point. Last year and to date there has been widespread consensus that we are facing a crisis in the residential construction industry and in housing. Many people are of the impression that this is due to a chronic shortage of loanable funds in the economy or of tight money. There may be some element of justification for this position, but I think it can also be said that it is not so much a case of shortage of loanable funds as the fact that existing loanable funds were being lent out to sectors of the economy that were more profitable. Last year, while we had a dramatic increase in industrial and commercial construction, we had a falling off in residential construction.
Very often an increase in the money supply is not what is required. Very often what is needed is a selective channeling of supplies of money, loanable funds, purchasing power-[DOT]-call it what you want-into particular sectors of our economy. At the present time when we have this crisis in housing and residential construction I submit that nothing short of massive injections of funds by direct channeling into residential construction will deal with the problem effectively.
To increase the money supply indiscriminately in the context of today would not necessarily deal with the problem of the downturn in residential construction starts and would, in fact, add to the problem of inflation. This is because these added funds would be attracted to higher return commercial construction and away from housing. So
Bank Act
there must be channeling. We are really facing somewhat of a problem of inflation. Even though many of the indices show a turning away from the spectre of inflation which we faced last year, the problem still lurks with us and is around the corner at all times.
As I say, the solution is not as simple as merely advocating an increase in the money supply and saying this will cure the problem, because attendant with it much thought must be given to matters of distribution, allocation, and so on.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I agree in part with those who advocate a greater degree of public, political or parliamentary control over our monetary system. I believe we have such control in large part now, but I have misgivings when I see provisions in this legislation to reduce the reserve requirements on the part of our commercial banks and, as I say, the ratio there seems to be an inverse one. The less the amount of reserves which commercial banks are required to hold with the central bank, the more is the reduction in public or parliamentary control and management within our monetary system.
Now I would like to make passing reference to the recommendation put before the committee just the other day by my colleague from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. I believe we should endorse a policy of some experimentation in our monetary and banking system. That is one reason why we are supporting this clause of the bill. There is nothing wrong with experimentation, if it is prudent and conducted under conditions of close control. In like vein the hon. member put forward the proposition that the government should give consideration to the feasibility and desirability of owning and operating a commercial bank, and that it consider the desirability of having one of our eight or nine chartered banks publicly owned. [DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
There is nothing rash or imprudent about that. Admittedly it would be a matter of experimentation. It certainly is in the public interest that we have a degree of experimentation in order to find out which innovations and which approaches are in fact the best ones and the ones most likely to be most beneficial so far as the public good is concerned.

speechtext: When the committee rose shortly after seven o'clock clause 72 was being considered.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words about clause 72 with regard to bank reserves, and then move an amendment.
When the Bank of Canada was established in 1934, a five-line section provided that the Bank of Canada had to maintain a reserve of at least 5 per cent of the value of deposit liabilities required in Canadian dollars. Following the 1944 decennial review, a 12 line paragraph said the same thing: "a 5 per cent reserve". Following the decennial review of 1954, the 5 per cent reserve rate was increased to 8 per cent in a section containing 37 lines. In 1967, after a decennial review which has lasted 13 years, since it is being made this year instead of in 1964, that same currency reserve takes up 97 lines and involves various types of rates for several kinds of deposits in the same banks. It is beyond understanding, Mr. Chairman.
The amendments of the 1934 and 1954 decennial reviews were very easy to understand, consisting of only a few lines and fixing the reserve at 5 per cent in one case and at 8 per cent, in the other. People could then understand something.
We now have a 12 per cent reserve, a 4 per cent reserve, another 8 per cent reserve and still another of 8 per cent, so many reserves that it is practically impossible to understand anything. I wonder why things have to be so complicated when it would be so easy to simplify them. It is practically incomprehensible. One must have a university degree to understand something and still, many with university degrees fail to understand anything.
The hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Tremblay) said earlier that financiers or bankers who appeared before the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs should have given me a course in political economy or financial economy. I think that several members opposite would need such a course. I feel the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane himself has still something to learn, even though he is an economist, because he does not have a clue about the whole system.
As a matter of fact, the present system is so complicated that something should surely be changed. We do not have to accept such
March 20, 1967



situations and complications. We should explain those things as simply as possible. Whether it be a rate of 8, 5 or 10 per cent, we should know that it is a rate and only a figure. There is no need for ten figures to complicate the system. It is so complicated that even experts, such as the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane, find it difficult to understand. Many people should take these courses, because you can take my word for it, the more it goes, the more complicated it gets and the more difficult it is to understand. The population is being held in ignorance, people are prevented from understanding anything in all this and the whole truth is being hidden from the population of Canada, as far as financial affairs are concerned. And the great economists such as my hon. friend opposite, who are supposed to do something to enlighten the population, are doing everything they can to keep them in the depth of ignorance, the deepest in the country.
So, Mr. Chairman, I say to the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane you have responsibilities, and I am asking you to honour them, because the population will not long tolerate private preserves as in the past, it will not tolerate things the people should have known and that no one knows today.
Mr. Chairman, the same experts who have had classical education and taken university courses do not understand anything any longer; they do not know what to believe about cash reserves, about bank reserves; the more complicated it gets, the more confusing it becomes for the people who have no business understanding anything about this medley of bank acts, particularly when it is desirable to prove that the banks are not creating either money or credit.
So, Mr. Chairman, I move: That section 72 be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"72. The bank shall maintain a cash reserve in the form of notes of, and deposits in Canadian currency with, the Bank of Canada.
Such reserve shall not be less than ten per cent of all its deposit liabilities in respect of all its depositors, for the first year of the present Act, and shall be raised by ten per cent each year, thereafter, until it becomes one hundred per cent of its deposit liabilities.
Such reserve shall be calculated on the monthly average of the bank deposit liabilities."
Mr. Chairman, by passing this amendment, we would allow chartered banks to finance private enterprise and enable the government to assume their responsibilities; we would enable the government to give the Bank of
Bank Act
Canada what it needs to assume its own responsibilities and then the Bank of Canada would finance public projects and with interest-free money. When we talk about interest-free money, we know that there are going to be administration costs, but we know that those administration costs, for instance, will not be like under the present system. Within the space of a dozen years, we have doubled the capital and this is nonsense.
When the hon. Minister of Finance and Receiver General (Mr. Sharp) says there will be administration costs, this will not change anything. The administration will not cost twice as much, if we know how to administer.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I move this amendment. I have copies of it here, if someone wishes to send them to the Chair. I read it a while ago, so I do not have to read it again.

The minister said:
I have been trying for most of my adult life to understand Social Credit, I have not succeeded very well. But what has puzzled me even more is how anyone could accept these doctrines.

I also believe that ridicule is a way of hiding total ignorance. The hon. member for Compton-Frontenac moved an amendment whereby the bank shall maintain a 10 per cent reserve which shall be gradually raised by 10 per cent per year until its deposit liabilities become 100 per cent. By this process the operations of the bank would be restrained to a certain extent and a totally new credit would be created. Under the clause as it stands at present the bank can maintain 4 per cent to 8 per cent reserves in different sectors, which allows the chartered banks to give credit up to approximately $4 billion without requiring larger savings deposits.

Not too long ago, in 1965, I was called a prophet by the former minister of finance, the hon. member for Davenport. I made the prophecy, and I am still here, but he has changed his seat. My prophecy was made in May of 1965 and anybody who wishes can look it up and check it. At that time the minister lowered the reserves from 8 per cent to 7 per cent, thus allowing the chartered banks to extend loans up to the sum of $1,428 million. This prevented the government from restricting credit in May and early June of 1965. The government planned to have an election in the fall following which credit restrictions would be imposed. If the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane would care to look back to the time in 1965 he would see that there was an election on November 8, 1965 immediately followed by credit restrictions.
In the months of May, June and July the government even cut down expenditures on government construction in Montreal. It tightened the screws wherever it could. That is what I prophesied in May of 1965 and the former minister of finance called me a prophet. I did not want to be a prophet. All I did was to think logically on the basis of a system which had operated in the same way for the past 40 or 50 years. It will not change today. The present system is following a definite pattern. Some amendments or changes will have to be brought in before the situation can change. At present we live from one crisis to another. We have a high rate of unemployment, credit restrictions, and wide fluctuations in our economy. At one time we have a period of inflation and at another time a period of recession. I might say to the hon. member for Mata-pedia-Matane (Mr. Tremblay) that I do not object in the least to the banks being allowed to charge interest on their loans. It is their privilege. By lending money they help and we must pay for goods and services.

They could operate like the caisse populaire. In private enterprise, when things do not work out successfully, it is because the goods or services are useless.
Nowadays, the Canadian taxpayer or citizen has to go and kneel before the financial or banking institutions because their system does not allow him to live otherwise. That is where the problem lies.
If we had a system in which human beings are shown some respect, chartered banks could exist if there was need for them. They say themselves that they are private undertakings operated to make profits. If they did not make a profit, I am sure they would
be intelligent enough to close shop. And I would not be too unhappy about it.
However, there might be more competition than we have now. Why? Because the individual would not be caught by the throat, or constantly strangled. He could not be told: Go that way or else you're done for. That is what our present system does.
If we could choose between the private and the public sectors, but that is not possible.
I would say to the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane that if he planted potatoes in the school yard, he would be told: You, listen, your potatoes, your onions, your garden, they do not belong to you. As an individual, no, collectively, yes. Then, if you do not have the right to plant potatoes in the school yard, how is it that they have the right to take your savings, as an individual, to pay for a public undertaking? And charge interest to you for a thing belonging to the whole society.
Why not use what is a public property, a public credit, that is the Bank of Canada, to finance the public sector of the economy. I have no objection to private enterprise being financed by private credit or private banks, with interest, because the people have something to do with production.
There is a productive field and a non-productive field; the service sector which is the public field.
A highway produces nothing. It can help the private sector to produce more, but the highway itself produces nothing. After its construction, it starts to depreciate until it disappears completely.
Yet, when depreciation starts, interest begins on the other side of the balance. Ultimately we have a road which has no value at all but there is the capital to repay, and interest which multiplied, which doubled, tripled, depending on circumstances, during 20 or 30 years of payment.
The hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) quoted the example of the Jacques Cartier bridge which was built in that way. After a given amount had been paid for the construction of the Jacques Cartier bridge, it was again paid for in interest. There is still interest owing, as well as the cost of the whole bridge. And that is not a productive sector, it is a public service. Public affairs are financed by interest, capital and money taken from the private sector. Why does the

-As we shall show later, the creation of money has an important role to play in the achievement of economic objectives;

And this is most interesting:

Mr. Chairman, that is not a solution. The solution lies in the equilibrium which must exist between the true production of goods and services and the purchasing power in the hands of consumers. When the consumers have the purchasing power, there is no need to worry, demand follows and the products are taken up by consumption. That is what the Creditistes have been advocating for 35 years. Destroying what is good will not improve the lot of those who live in shacks for instance. It is possible in Canada to give everyone decent and healthy housing.

You cannot uplift the employee by crushing the employer. You cannot uplift the little man by bringing down the big ones.
What Lincoln said at that time, Mr. Chairman, is as true to day as it was then, over a hundred years ago. That is why we are saying: Instead of trying as we always do in this house, and throughout Canada, instead of trying to tame men, women and children according to the whims of the financial system, let us once and for all, tame the financial system and make it serve the human beings which make up Canada, a Canada which, in the end, must bring security with freedom to each and every one of its citizens.
Mr. Chairman, that is the perspective in which we see the possibility and the urgency of amending the financial system, not in order to set one class against another or to make some people hate each other, but to create a united Canada, where Canadians feel at home and will always feel at home, where they will acquire financial independence through their bank which we call the Bank of Canada.

This afternoon someone quoted the following statement made by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance and Receiver General (Mr. Chretien):
Money does not grow on trees. It must be obtained either as taxes from taxpayers, or as loans.
Those are the only two methods found by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance and Receiver General when it comes to formulating the budget of the government: to take money, either as taxes out of the pockets of the public, or as loans.
Well, Mr. Chairman, this afternoon I heard the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) say a very clear sentence, which is a very good illustration of the problem, and I wonder whether the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance and Receiver General, by recalling this, or at least by having recalled to him what happened at the beginning of the war, will not realize that there are other monetary sources. That is what happened when the war broke out in 1939.
They are certainly not going to make us believe, Mr. Chairman, that when the Canadian government wanted to finance a war, which cost it about $14 billion, it got that kind of money from the pockets of Canadian citizens. No there was no money in there. Canadians certainly did not have the $14 billion required to finance the war.
In the United States, the situation was no better. The beginning of the war was for them the end of a depression. There was no more money in the United States to finance everything that the Americans spent during the 1939-45 war than there was in Canada
[Mr. Gregoire.l
before the war. Therefore we could not have borrow it or find it somewhere else to wage States since the Americans themselves had to borrow it or find it somewhere else to wage their war.
We could not borrow it either from France or Italy or Germany or England; on the contrary, we were lending money to England. We were able to find money during the war, which was quite a feat, and yet when war began, the government was dead broke, as well as the provinces, the municipalities, and the school boards, and Canadian citizens were in the midst of an economic crisis, they lived on relief with meager amounts which barely allowed them to exist.
Suddenly, overnight, a madman in Europe declared war; Canada found money to buy cannons, cannon balls, planes, warships; it found some more to lend England billions of dollars during the six years the war lasted. Suddenly money was found, not in the pockets of the Canadian people, because they did not have any money, they were dead broke.
Therefore, Canadian citizens did not pay for the 1939-45 war, nor for the loans to England, with their taxes. No, and we could not borrow from the United States or England since we were lending them money, nor from Germany or Italy. So where did we get it? How is it that during a period of depression, from 1929 to 1939, during ten years, the government allowed itself to let all the people of Canada in misery and, suddenly, when war was declared, the funds needed were found? There was always money to finance the war and it was never necessary to do it on finance. I have never heard of a Canadian airman dropping bombs on Germany and then sending the bill to the finance company saying that he had 24 months to pay. Indeed, bombs were not paid through finance companies but were dropped free of charge on the Germans. They just got them, nothing more. Money was found for all kinds of things, whereas money was scarce during the depression.

subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the hon. Minister of Finance for having suggested that the house study again clause 69, because it had been passed Friday last. Inadvertently I did not rise in time to put forward my amendment.
Since the Minister of Finance has helped me to have this clause reconsidered, maybe he will vote with us.
Mr. Chairman, section 1 of clause 69 reads as follows:
(1) Where in the opinion of the minister an amount set aside or reserved by the bank out of income, either by way of write-down of the value of assets or appropriation for the purpose of meeting losses on loans, bad or doubtful debts, depreciation in the value of assets other than bank premises or other contingencies, is in excess of the reasonable requirements of the bank, having regard to all the circumstances, the Minister shall notify the Minister of National Revenue of the amount so set aside and of the amount of such excess.
That means that this is left up to the bank and to its point of view, if it is a reasonable one.
Then, who is going to determine whether or not it is reasonable? It is a vague clause. I believe it is most important when it has to do with secret reserves, hidden reserves or indiscreet reserves, call them what you like. There are excessive amounts, there are quite high amounts which the Minister of Finance, I think, does not know because I asked him when he was before the committee whether he was aware of those reserves and he said yes. I asked him what was the amount of those reserves and he could not answer me. He did not know the amount of the reserves and it is very plainly stated in the clause that the Minister of Finance cannot take any action with regard to the matter of secret or secondary reserves.

March 20, 1967
Bank Act
Banks already have enough reserves of all kinds that they must not be given a free hand with the other secret reserves, which would be limited only by their own judgment, under the present act, for "The reasonable requirements of the bank."
Who is going to determine what are reasonable requirements? The Royal Bank, for instance, in 1933, during the depression, transferred, in that one year, $15 million from its general reserves to its secondary, secret and hidden reserves, as reported on page 306 of the French version of the proceedings of the standing committee on banking and commerce, in 1934. Page 4 contains many other monstrous statements concerning secret bank reserves.
The Minister of Finance told the house on two or three occasions that, for the first time, chartered banks would be forced to disclose their secret reserves. Now that deposit insurance has been introduced, banks have even less reason to have unlimited secret reserves, left at the discretion of bank directors.
Surely, the limit is set high enough-I think it is one half of 1 per cent-when we know that deposit insurance easily covers a guarantee of 1/30 of 1 per cent, as insurance premium, of all the deposits in Canada and of companies that want or have to pay deposit insurance premiums.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
As far as paragraph (2) of the same clause, just imagine, sir, the condescension necessary when it comes to keeping a close watch on the bankers' scheme. Just refer to the wording of the clause: this is not an invention of mine:
Nothing in subsection (1) shall be construed to give the minister any jurisdiction ... with regard to amounts set aside, reserved or transferred to any reserve-
Thus there are reserved, sacred, hidden, direct or indirect accounts, whatever you call them.
How much did the banks hide in 1966? How much did they put aside in the last ten years? For what reasons do we allow banks to have hidden reserves? Did all large corporations have hidden reserves, for different amounts in 1967? There are many other companies, many other institutions which would surely be entitled also, Mr. Chairman, to indirect reserves, internal reserves or hidden reserves.
I note that clause 69 of the bill is similar to section 68 of the present act and there is no evidence that banks will be obliged to state their secret reserves in the future, any more

than in the past. Why did the Minister of Finance state to this house, and I quote:
Banks will have to give a detailed statement of their earnings and expenses, and, for the first time, of their hidden reserves.
In your own mother tongue, I quote No. 8 of your principal resolutions:

The banks to reveal revenue and expenses in detail and for the first time their hidden reserves.

The minister should tell us under what clause of Bill No. C-222 the banks are forced to reveal their hidden reserves. Whom can we trust if we are deceived by the Minister of Finance on such an important matter as the presentation in the house of Bill No. C-222 on banks and banking?
In 1934, Mr. Chairman, when the Bank of Canada was created, in the same committee on banking and commerce, at pages 305 to 308 of the Minutes of Proceedings, there was talk of making such reserves. In a strange way, several questions by hon. members remained unanswered by the bankers. It is just like today, and it is the best proof that the stronger is not the government but the banker who hides everything he wants from the people, the government and his shareholders. I could give many other examples of hidden reserves by banks and big corporations. But what is the use, Mr. Chairman?
I will not say any more about that because I cannot do any more to force the minister to speak and tell the people the truth. I used all the means at my disposal. He speaks neither French nor English, but an incomprehensible language.
In another statement made to the House of Commons by the Minister of Finance, one could read in clause 5 on page 9:
We propose to require from the banks that they reveal to the public for the first time their hidden reserves made up with taxable income.
The minister himself said that. And in his own language:

We propose to require the banks to reveal to the public for the first time their hidden reserves created out of taxable income.

Mr. Chairman, is this the same Minister of Finance? Is he still prepared to make the same statement? Is he prepared to include in the bill the clause he had advocated requiring banks to disclose their hidden reserves?
March 20, 1967

I will now move my amendment, Mr. Chairman, for I do not want to extend the debate too long. It reads as follows:
(1)	That the words in "reasonable requirements of the bank" in section 69 (1) be deleted and replaced by the words "i of 1 per cent of its deposit liabilities".
(2)	That subsection (2) be deleted and replaced by the following: "Any amount in excess of the authorized reserve shall be immediately declared as taxable profits of the bank by the Minister of National Revenue".

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to support to a certain extent the amendment moved by my colleague the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Latulippe).
It is obvious that in clause 69, what we used to call hidden reserves, are not hidden any longer today, but what I object to is that the banks are empowered to put up a reserve for losses and that such reserve, whether the bank incurs losses or not, is exempt from tax.
Mr. Chairman, if any business man, any store owner, any automobile dealer, any furniture salesman, any home builder, were putting up reserves against losses, they would have to pay taxes. But the bank gets more benefits than the businessman. The ordinary bank has an additional privilege, it is exempt from tax, not on its losses, but on what it declares to be a reserve for losses, whether or not it incurs any losses, and that is what I object to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the committee will be aware that when we approved clause 60 of the present bill we did approve the following. I should like to draw attention to paragraph (2)(c) of clause 60. Subclause 2 reads as follows:
At every annual general meeting of the shareholders, the outgoing directors shall submit a statement (hereinafter called the "annual statement"), which shall present fairly the financial position of the bank for the financial year immediately preceding the meeting, and shall contain-
I will read paragraph (c):
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
-a statement of accumulated appropriations for losses of the bank for the financial year, showing the information in the form specified in schedule P-
Bank Act
I will not read the rest of that paragraph. Schedule P provides for the revelation for the first time, as I said before, and as referred to by the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac, of inner or so-called hidden reserves. This act does in fact carry out the undertaking that I made in the house that for the first time the inner reserves of banks will be publicly revealed. Clause 69 with which we are now dealing provides that I shall continue, as I have in the past, to have some control over the amounts of those reserves that are to be considered taxable or non-taxable. I submit it is better for public administration to have that judgment made by the Minister of Finance rather than by the Minister of National Revenue, who is concerned with taxation but not with banking questions.
In respect of the particular amendment moved by the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac let me assure him that the kind of inner reserves dealt with in clause 69 have nothing to do with the deposit liabilities of banks. These have to do with their investments and they are reserves against the possibility of losses. Therefore I submit, Mr. Chairman, that these amendments do not fulfil the purposes of clause 69 and should be rejected.

subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Why grant a special treatment to the banks and say to them: "Whether you lose money or not, it does not matter, because you are entitled to a reserve for losses; furthermore you have tax exemptions". And it is also indicated in schedule P to which the minister referred a moment ago:
Accumulated appropriations at beginning of year, general-Tax-paid-Total.
In no other field of trade or business would the Minister of National Revenue say: "Gentlemen, you are entitled to an appropriation for losses, for example, and it will be tax-free. It is obvious that if a loss is real, the interested party will find an arrangement and will have a delay of five years to substract that loss from its income tax report. The loss will be spread over a period of five years. But for the bank it comes to more than that. Even if it has not sustained a loss, it will pay no tax on its reserve for losses. This is irregular and I cannot accept it. I believe that if we remove this idea or notion that appropriations for losses should be tax-free-and this is where I am slightly at variance with my friend, the member for Compton-Frontenac

March 20, 1967
Bank Act
(Mr. Latulippe)-I would ask him to forget the i per cent and say that, since the reserves are now open and known, the bank may appropriate whatever it wishes for losses, it does not matter, provided it pays income tax. It would then be a reserve such as those of any business concern. The purpose of section 69 is to prevent banks from having reserves that are too high since they are tax free. But even if the reserve is not too high, the bank should not enjoy any unfair privilege. As soon as the bank looses money, it should be allowed to deduct it from its income tax like all the other business concerns, over a five year period, but it should not be tax exempt for losses not incurred. A bank should not be told: Build up a tax reserve which is tax-free. It is on that point that I support the amendment of my colleague, the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Langlois). I wonder if the Minister of Finance does not find our request reasonable. After all, banks are not to so much to be pitied. The saying "as sound as the bank" is very significant. That means it is a well-established institution. I wonder why it should need preferential treatment or such a favour which is not given to any other business. There are businessmen here, doctors who may lose accounts, lawyers who may be unable to collect certain fees; dentists who may be unable to collect certain bills. They are not taxed, it is true, but the lawyer, for instance, is not told: Take $5,000 and put it aside as a reserve against losses. Whether he loses it or not does not matter. According to the legislation as it stands, it is just a reserve on which the bank is not taxed.
The hon. member for Compton-Frontenac mentions one half of one per cent. I think that in committee, the question was put. I think it was said that bank losses, if I am not mistaken, my memory may fail me, but I think the losses were under one tenth of one per cent. I would not swear to it, I do not have the report of this committee with me, but possibly the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron), who attended the committee as I did, could tell me whether it was approximately this amount that was mentioned. If my memory serves me well, the losses were of one tenth of 1 percent. Then, if no tax is levied on this, quite right. However, if we charge one half of one per cent-for a bank, this is a great deal. On a business turnover of 18 billion per annum, 1 per cent represents $1,800 million, and half of one per cent is $900 million. If they are allowed reserves in con-

nection with which we declare: "On this, you will have no taxes to pay", well, perhaps- If we were doing this for all concerns, if everybody were on an equal footing, personally, I am for this, but when there is favour for some one and disfavour for the others, I am against that.
This is why I am asking whether the minister would agree to delete this discriminatory clause. I think that the request is perfectly logical and reasonable; the banks are not to be pitied, they are not in the red, they need no other favours from the government, since I figure that they have enough; then the tax is always removed. And on this I could reach an agreement with my friends of the New Democratic Party, who say at all times taxes should not be paid by the little fellow but by the big fellow; well, are not the big fellows in Canada the chartered banks? If so, let us not grant them special favours concerning income tax; under section 60(2) and Schedule (p) they get some valuable favours: they are told: "Gentlemen, do put aside a reserve for losses, and on this, whether you lose it or not, you will not be charged income tax." Then I wonder whether the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) would have a few remarks to make on these points, whether he would not be prepared to accept what we are asking from him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there seems to be some misunderstanding about the basis of our taxation system. There is nothing special about this clause. All businesses have the right to have reserves against bad debts. That is all this is. The reason that discretion is given to the minister is to see that the amounts set aside are not excessive, and that is the spirit in which it is administered. The inspector general of banks advises me every year of the amounts set aside, and he advises me whether in his opinion they are excessive. In my opinion there is greater control over taxation of banks than there is over taxation of other institutions.
