subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have two amend-

March 20, 1967
Bank Act
ments to this clause. The first is as follows. I move:
That paragraph (a) of subclause (3) of clause 53 be amended by striking out the following words in line 38 on page 31 "in right of Canada or", and also by striking out the word "either" where it appears in line 40.
I am quite sure that the minister realizes the significance of this amendment, because it deals with the question I raised with him during the committee hearings, and again the other day when I was speaking in the committee of the whole. I am proposing this amendment, not to alter any powers that the government of Canada has at this moment but to prevent the minister from divesting the government of Canada of the power of making an investment in a commercial bank.
I feel it is important at this particular juncture that the government of Canada should retain that power in its hands. I set out the reasons for this the other day when I was speaking in the house. At this time I would merely like to underline again the possibility of having to use this power in connection with a circumstance which still could possibly cause some trouble with our American neighbours.
I am not at all sure, as I said in the committee, that we have solved the problem of the Mercantile Bank by the only course left open to us at the time, in passing an amendment which I seconded to give the bank five years to expand their shares and make them attractive to Canadian investors. I have the uneasy suspicion that at the end of five years we will find the bank not anxious to divest itself of its shares, and may present the government of Canada with the very difficult task of asking the bank to shrink its shares back to this twenty to one ratio, or to get rid of 75 per cent of its shares.
[DOT] (10:40 p.m.)
I have an idea that if at this time the Minister of Finance for Canada were to recognize this and say that he accepts this amendment, that action of his might be noted in New York and Washington, and the conclusion might be drawn that the Canadian Minister of Finance was retaining in his hip pocket a club which he might see fit to use if necessary in five years. For that reason I urge the committee to support my amendment, to leave in the hands of the government of Canada the right to invest in a bank.
The other day my hon. friend from Edmonton West, as I noted from reading Hansard, though I did not hear him, meant to say, I think, that I have an obsession. He told me
[Mr. Carr*pron (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands) 1
the other day-even today-that I have a coy way of using words. I do not wish to say this to my friend, but he has an incorrect way of using them. He used the word "fetish" quite incorrectly. I suspect that he meant to say I had an obsession with the nationalization of the banks of Canada, and using "fetish" was quite incorrect. It was incorrect even in its original Ashanti form in West Africa, to say nothing of its modern psychological connotation.

subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: Smart.

subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: One has to be smart with me, my hon. friend. I have no obsession with the nationalization of the banks; but I do have an obsession, and it is not shared with my hon. friend from Edmonton West. My obsession is that every institution in our society must serve the welfare of the Canadian people. I have another obsession, that no one has the right to be allowed to exploit his fellow citizens, that no one has the God given right to make money out of any operation of our society, or to assume that this is a privilege we grant to certain people under certain terms, a privilege that can be amended or withdrawn at any time. No institution serves the welfare of the Canadian people if it is for the aggrandizement of only a few of our citizens.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I say a brief word about this proposed amendment. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands is relating it to the experience of the Mercantile Bank. Mr. Chairman, if the Mercantile Bank is unable to dispose of its shares to Canadians it would be better that it remain as a very small operation, as it is today. Certainly, if that is the position of the Mercantile Bank, then I have no quarrel.
On the other hand if the government is to make an investment in a bank, a chartered bank, or a bank operating under one of our charters, in my opinion it should not have other private shareholders. Therefore if we are to embark on that course of action-and this is an arguable case; I think there is a good deal to be said for having a government-owned bank-let us do so not by inadvertence or indirection, but let us do it as the result of a positive decision by this parliament to form a bank for that purpose.
I am therefore opposed to the amendment proposed by my hon. friend. It seems to me that if we are to change our policy and have a government bank in competition with pri-
March 20, 1967

vate banks, let us do it, not now, but let us charter a bank for that purpose.

subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: I could not agree more with the minister. I am not proposing that we change our present position; he is proposing the change. That change is to prohibit the government of Canada from ever following this course of investing in a bank. Certainly, if this bill passes as it is worded now, Her Majesty in the right of Canada would be prohibited from investing in a chartered bank.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: That is right.

subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: Then it is the minister who is changing the position which presently prevails, because the power now lies in his hands or in the hands of the government of Canada, and will continue to do so until this bill is passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: What this clause does is to prevent Her Majesty in the right of Canada from acquiring any shares in a chartered bank included in the schedule to this bill. If parliament were to decide that it would form a government bank to operate like a chartered bank, it could certainly do so and would not be bound by this act.

subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
This does not explain why the minister and the government found it necessary to include this prohibition. The fact is that under the present Bank Act there is no such inhibition which would prevent the government entering into a partnership, if you like, with a chartered bank or buying any shares in a chartered bank which in the public interest it believed would be desirable.
What my hon. friend is saying to the minister is that his amendment is not the one which proposes a change in the present law; it is this new clause which proposes a change, and I have heard no explanation why this change should be made. The minister has not told us why it should be necessary for this parliament to tie its hands for the next ten years. It may be that the government of the day will not wish to use the powers it presently has to buy shares in a chartered bank. But why should we now decide that in no circumstances in the next ten years will the government of Canada be able to do so, no matter what the circumstances may be?
The minister should explain to the committee why he found it necessary to include this provision in the bill. What are the circumstances in 1967 which differ from those of 1965 or 1957 when this prohibition was not contained in our banking laws? What has 23033-9001
Bank Act
happened to make this provision necessary? The minister should tell us what moved him to propose this fundamental change in the banking law. If his explanation is that because he wished to prevent the provinces from doing so he is making things even, then I suggest this is the type of equality which does not appeal to any logical mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
The change was made because we wanted to prohibit any government, whether provincial or federal or foreign, from owning shares in a chartered bank. We do not think it is appropriate to the kind of banking system we have that governments should be shareholders in banks. As far as I know, the government of Canada has no shares in a chartered bank and never has had any. Perhaps by inadvertence it may have got into some pension fund, or something like that but, as I have said, I do not know of it.
[DOT] (10:50 p.m.)
I would come back to my original point that if the parliament of Canada wants the government of Canada to invest in the shares of a bank it should authorize them specifically for some purpose and not have the government in the position of becoming an investor in an existing chartered bank. I believe this is thoroughly consistent with the whole philosophy of the act.

subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
The thing that puzzles me, Mr. Chairman, is why the minister does not admit that this is a case of the government biting off its nose to spite its face. The last time the Bank Act came up for decennial review this question did not arise. No change was made at that time in the concept of ownership of bank shares, or laws in that respect, and I presume those laws were the same since banking legislation first came into being in this country.
Why does the minister not admit that it was because the government of B.C. expressed an interest in acquiring the shares of a bank that this whole question came to the fore? Why does he not admit that the government of Canada never thought of this question until the government of the province from which I come expressed some interest in the idea of developing a regional bank in which the government of that province would have some say, so far as its management and policy were concerned?
I do not suggest that we should enter into a debate on that question at this time, nor does the amendment moved by my colleague from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands suggest that we do so; but certainly so far the minister has

March 20, 1967
Bank Act
failed to impress me with the logic of there being any parallel between the views the government has with regard to provincial governments or foreign governments holding bank shares, and leaving within the power of the federal government the right to hold shares in the name of the body which I have always understood to be the authority over monetary and fiscal policy in Canada. I think the amendment carefully emphasizes that particular distinction in the concept of money and banking business.

subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
I too am puzzled by this problem. I listened with interest to the discussions which took place concerning the Mercantile Bank and the desire of the Canadian government to obtain Canadian control over that institution. The government might have to set up a crown agency to buy that stock if Canadians as individuals do not buy it.

For this reason the government should reserve the right to buy the stock through a crown corporation operating in the right of Her Majesty. Personally I feel this provision should be left in the bill, also covering the right of a province.
I would think, if there really is a desire to implement the idea of establishing a method to obtain Canadian control over foreign owned financial institutions, that a start should be made at least in respect of the one bank in question. If you leave in the one exception where no shares are to be held by a government, then obviously you are taking away the machinery which would make possible what has been suggested. When one considers the proposition of exempting Her Majesty from having any control, he can better understand the government's inability to obtain Canadian control over other financial institutions, including near banks and insurance companies.

Evidently the minister is sincere in his wish that the Mercantile Bank eventually will flow into Canadian control. 1 believe, if this particular clause in its present form, or with the limitation against provincial government ownership, is to be retained, that a clause should be included which at least would allow the minister to establish a corporation which eventually would be able to buy the stock, which may not always be easily disposed of. It may not be easy to persuade Canadians to buy this stock, particularly with the pressure which would be applied in a situation where it was desired to unload that stock on Canadians.
I believe the minister should give a better explanation of the reason he is not willing at least to leave with the federal government the right to establish a crown corporation. If the government itself does not wish to buy the stock it should allow an agency to assume the financial control which, in my opinion, the Bank Act is designed to do. If the minister is unwilling to provide the machinery to make it possible, then I think we should have passed the previous legislation without amendment, because this certainly will not accomplish the desire of most Canadians eventually to obtain control of one foreign owned bank through purchase of the stock by Canadians, or through government purchase of the outstanding stock.

Mr. Chairman, I am not too worried about the public interest. We as Canadians made an agreement in 1953 to grant a charter to a foreign concern. Let us be honest and live up to that agreement which was granted, rightly or wrongly, to this
Bank Act
concern. Perhaps if we were asked to do this again we would not do it. We did do it with our eyes open, without any stipulations at all. Then we allowed that foreign concern to sell its shares to another foreign concern. Canada is respected throughout the world as a country which lives up to its agreements. Certainly we would not want to be considered as having a preference for a Dutch concern over an American concern. We are very dependant upon United States capital and its commerce, and we would not want to create an impression that we preferred Dutch firms to American firms. By passing this clause we are taking away the one safeguard that still lies in the hands of the Canadian government. We must live up to our commitment. Whatever the foreign concerns are, we should not show preference to one over another. So if the charter was good for the Dutch in 1953 it is good for the Americans today, and we are not going to allow those shares to devaluate. We will not deliberately, through a misunderstanding at the transfer of those shares, force their value down. Surely we will live up to a prior commitment, regardless of whether it was right or wrong.

speechtext: I do not see any reference to 10 years in clause 57 such as was the case in respect of the B.X.F. group, which has proven to have consisted of of poor financial managers. It was given 10 years, whereas the Mercantile Bank, which does not have to prove its ability in financial management, was given only five years. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
The Mercantile Bank does not have to dispose of any of its shares, if it does not wish to. If it wishes to remain a small operation, as it is today, it does not have to distribute any shares. The provisions of the law, to which we have not yet come, place restrictions upon any bank whose shares are owned to the extent of more than 25 per cent by any single individual, but if the bank chooses to remain small it may do so and retain 100 per cent of its ownership.
What we are talking about here is the incorporation of a new bank in Canada. I do believe that there should be some discretion to assist Canadians in establishing new banks. I believe we need more new banks and there will be many applications. I doubt whether it will be possible at the outset to distribute the shares so widely that all the banks will be able to comply from the first day with the 10 per cent requirement. It seems to me that under the circumstances 10 years is reasonable. Of course this is always a question of judgment. All these orders have been tabled for a long time. They were discussed to some extent in the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs.
We are not now confronting parliament with some very special, hidden arrangement. The details have been well known. They have been discussed in the newspapers and elsewhere. While some questions may be raised about some of the shareholders, it is hardly surprising that some difficulties should be ex-

perienced in getting a new bank started. This is one of the reasons why I doubt that a lot of the argument we have heard today, about the enormous profitability of banks, is justified. We are seeing evidence that it is very difficult indeed to get new banks started. Therefore I believe we should encourage them as far as possible, and permit them to have in excess of 10 per cent of their shares in the hands of individual shareholders. To me this seems a very small concession to make in order to get a bank successfully established.

I should like to ask the minister why this restriction was put on the Mercantile Bank in particular. Was there a limit put on the Dutch interests, then we must conclude that the gov-back in 1953? I would not like to think that a country as big as Canada but dependant upon the economy of the U.S. and its ups and downs, as has been proven in the past, has acted in an anti-American manner by placing a limit on the size of a charter that was granted back in 1953 and forcing that company to divest itself of 75 per cent of its interests.
This suggests to me that the government is definitely anti-American. If the minister wishes to deny that, then I hope he will do so because I am very proud of our good relations with the U.S.
There is another question with regard to the management of the B.I.F. group which I should like to address to the minister. Would he admit now that only a very cursory examination was given by this department to the financial ability of the B.I.F. group before a licence was granted to the Bank of Western Canada? I would like to think that the minister gave this question a lot of thought before the charter was granted and the licence issued by his department.
We have seen Mr. Coyne, who is a very honest individual. I do not think there is a

However, he certainly did not do the Bank of Western Canada any good by raising the furore he raised last fall. He did maintain his basic integrity. I wonder if the minister will now admit that his department should have made a much more thorough examination of the financial ability of that group before he permitted it to have a charter? I know several ministers with whom I have talked in private who have told me that a bank charter is a very special and very valuable commodity in this country of ours. Just the charter alone is a very special and very valuable commodity. Surely, now that we have seen the difficulties into which the B.I.F. group has fallen, when we have seen that they are $1.4 million short, the minister could honestly declare to this house that in the future a much more thorough examination will be made of the financial management capabilities of a group asking for a charter. Surely this is not asking too much of the minister before this clause passes, to say that he is now convinced that the examination of the management of the bank was not enough. The examination should have been far more thorough.
The minister should be able to say that in the granting of bank charters in the future a much more detailed study will take place before the inspector general of banks comes before a committee and says, "Yes, the committee can rest assured that the management is sound and has ability". We even saw Mr. Stevens, the main spokesman for the B.I.F. group, come before us eight months later and say he was a little short. He wanted to go down to the United States to pick up the $1.4 million because there he would get the money and also experienced advice. Surely there has been a shortfall in the examination the minister's department has made. I should like him to say that in so far as future charters are concerned, there will be a much more thorough examination.
The minister may ask why I am so concerned. I am concerned because very close to

$6.3 million was money invested from western Canada, which money was invested on the strength of the understanding that the management had been examined, that James Coyne was in a group of very wise, shrewd financial men. This is why I am so concerned. I am firmly convinced that we westerners, as James Coyne said five months ago, were sucked in along with him. Now we are going to have to ride that out.
We have heard lately that the stock has changed hands and gone to Montreal from Toronto. I ask the Minister of Finance, has the inspector general of banks or his department examined this new group to see whether they are capable of managing a bank? Can we expect within a few weeks, five months or five years, that the whole bundle will go somewhere else? Surely the minister now realizes that his department did not examine the management ability of this group. As a result of that, the people of western Canada invested $6.3 million, and they find they have not had the money to use. It has been placed in trust, so to speak. The shares were bought at $15 per share, and the value has dropped substantially below that. If those shares were placed on the market, that would be the result and nobody on that side of the house can deny it.
We were sucked in, along with James Coyne, who invested only $7,500 in the bank. His intent was honest, but he found he could not live with the Stevens group from Toronto. Last fall he did not ask any questions. He did not point out anything factual to the committee, but he felt firmly this was going to happen. He raised a great furore and cleared his own name. But there is still a huge amount of money invested in that concern in western Canada. Does the minister realize that there was a shortfall in that concern which was examined by his department? Can he assure the house that before granting charters in the future a more thorough examination will take place? Because that is an important point.
Charters were granted in B.C. and others may be granted in Quebec and Ontario. I would not like to see the minister agree to granting a charter to a firm which had ten years to divest itself of its interest among aunts, uncles and brothers-in-law. That is what Mr. Stevens did in Toronto, according to the evidence given in the committee last year. He spread his investment around in this way. Therefore I should like the minister to assure
